keyVerseText: I am the LORD your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, that ye should not be their bondmen; and I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright.
rootMeaning: The root word מוֹט (môwṭ) conveys the idea of a bar or pole that is associated with shaking or wavering, suggesting instability or movement. מוֹטָה (môwṭâh), the feminine form, builds on this root to mean a pole or bar, specifically a bar of a yoke, which is a wooden frame used to join oxen for labor. This literal sense of a bent or shaking pole enriches the understanding of a yoke not merely as a physical object but as a symbol of burden or restraint, emphasizing both the structural and figurative implications of control and oppression.
usageInScripture: The word מוֹטָה appears twelve times in Scripture, predominantly translated as 'bands,' 'yoke,' or 'staves,' reflecting its dual physical and symbolic usage. It often denotes the poles used to carry sacred objects, such as the ark, as well as the bars of a yoke representing subjugation or oppression. The consistency in translation between literal poles and figurative yokes illustrates the term’s flexibility in describing both tangible implements and the metaphorical burdens imposed on people, highlighting themes of bondage and deliverance.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מוֹטָה as both a physical yoke and a symbol of oppression deepens the biblical portrayal of God’s redemptive work in liberating His people. The imagery of breaking the bars or bands of the yoke underscores God’s power to remove spiritual and physical bondage, freeing believers from slavery to sin and external oppression. This word reminds Christians that deliverance is not only a historical event but a continual divine act, reflecting Christ’s work in breaking every yoke that enslaves humanity. Thus, מוֹטָה encapsulates the tension between captivity and freedom central to the gospel message.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 26:13 declares, 'I am the LORD your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, that ye should not be their bondmen; and I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright.' Here, מוֹטָה as 'bands of your yoke' powerfully conveys God’s intervention in breaking the physical and spiritual chains of slavery. The verse emphasizes God's role as deliverer who not only frees His people but also enables them to walk upright, symbolizing restored dignity and freedom. The word highlights the transformation from bondage to liberation that is foundational to faith in God’s covenantal care.
